title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - Manufacturing
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: Iran-linked hackers are rewriting plant-floor PLC logic and disabling safety functions
items.content_text: A federal advisory updated 22 July confirms the nightmare case for any plant floor: nation-state actors reaching inside programmable logic controllers and rewriting the code that runs the process. CISA, the FBI and NSA say Iran-affiliated actors are exploiting internet-exposed PLCs — Rockwell CompactLogix and Micro850, Siemens S7-1200 and Schneider Modicon M340 among them — by abusing legitimate engineering software to connect, exfiltrate project files, then modify or delete control logic, including Add-On Instructions, and manipulate HMI displays. In several cases they disabled shutdown and alarm logic, letting equipment drift into unsafe conditions with no operator warning. These are the same controllers and engineering workstations manufacturers run every day, so an exposed PLC or a compromised engineering laptop becomes a direct path to silently altered process logic and defeated safety interlocks.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: CISA / FBI / NSA joint advisory AA26-097A

items.title: FBI/EPA: attackers are hijacking internet-facing PLCs — the same controllers on your plant floor
items.content_text: In a 30 July public service announcement, the FBI and EPA said that since 27 July, water and wastewater utilities in at least seven states reported attackers reaching internet-exposed Rockwell/Allen-Bradley MicroLogix 1100 and 1400 PLCs, changing IP addresses and passwords to knock out monitoring and control — and in at least one case altering ladder logic across several sites, with reported effects including loss of pressure and flooding. The victims are water utilities, but the FBI stressed the same exposure applies to other branded PLCs — the internet-reachable Rockwell, Siemens and Schneider controllers manufacturers run every day. Any plant with a PLC or cellular field modem reachable from the internet should treat this as a direct warning.

_otthreatfeed.date_note: Issued 30 Jul 2026 — incidents reported since 27 Jul, ongoing; FBI has not publicly attributed

items.title: Coca-Cola’s Fairlife restarts US production after ransomware halt; data theft confirmed
items.content_text: Coca-Cola’s Fairlife subsidiary has resumed most production at its four US plants after a roughly ten-day shutdown triggered by a 16 July ransomware attack — a reminder that on the plant floor an IT compromise fast becomes an operations problem. In a 27 July update Coca-Cola said most operations were restored and confirmed attackers stole data; the Anubis group claimed the attack and listed the company on its leak site. US facilities were stopped precautionarily while Canadian operations continued. Manufacturing — and food and beverage especially, with just-in-time perishable output — offers attackers exactly the operational leverage that drives a fast payout.

_otthreatfeed.date_note: Disclosed 16 Jul 2026 — updated 27 Jul: production resumed, data theft confirmed

items.title: Dragos Q2 2026: manufacturing absorbs 65% of all industrial ransomware — and gangs disrupt output without ever touching a PLC
items.content_text: Dragos’ Q2 2026 industrial ransomware analysis counted 1,140 incidents against industrial organizations, up 12% from 1,020 in Q1, with manufacturing far and away the hardest hit at 747 incidents — 65% of the total — and the United States the most-targeted country at 431 (38%). Dragos’ key finding for plant operators is that crews rarely need control-system access to stop production: encrypting or crippling enterprise IT, ERP platforms and virtualization infrastructure is enough to idle lines, because scheduling, material flow and shipping all depend on those systems. Double-extortion remains standard — valid credentials, exposed remote access and data theft before encryption — and OT/control-system configs rarely restore from IT-style backups, so an IT-side hit can idle a line for weeks.

_otthreatfeed.source_name: Dragos Industrial Ransomware Analysis Q2 2026 / Help Net Security

items.title: Arista VeloCloud Orchestrator CVSS-10 command-injection exploited as a zero-day, now in KEV
items.content_text: CISA added CVE-2026-16812 to its KEV catalog on 27 July after the flaw — an unauthenticated OS command-injection bug in on-prem Arista VeloCloud (formerly VMware) SD-WAN Orchestrator, rated a maximum CVSS 10.0 — was exploited as a zero-day. A remote attacker with no credentials can run arbitrary commands on the appliance and take over the management plane. VeloCloud SD-WAN commonly stitches together multi-plant sites and carries remote-engineering and vendor access, so a compromised orchestrator hands an attacker a trusted path between corporate, plant IT and engineering networks. A patch is available; treat it as an emergency.

_otthreatfeed.date_note: Added to KEV 27 Jul 2026 — actively exploited

items.title: N-able N-central auth bypass exploited to hijack servers and reach managed endpoints — first patch failed
items.content_text: Attackers have been exploiting an authentication-bypass flaw (CVE-2026-18577, CVSS 8.2) in N-able’s widely-used N-central remote-monitoring-and-management platform since 1 August to take over on-prem servers, then use the built-in Take Control feature to reach every managed endpoint and register Cloudflare tunnels for persistent, firewall-transparent access. It is a bypass of an earlier fix (CVE-2026-18556), and N-able’s first hotfix proved incomplete — a second hotfix (build 2026.3.1.7, hardened 6 Aug) is required even if the first was applied. CISA added it to KEV on 3 August with a three-day federal deadline. For manufacturers this is the classic managed-services blast radius: an RMM that reaches plant IT and engineering workstations becomes an attacker’s route onto the floor.

_otthreatfeed.date_note: Exploited since 1 Aug 2026 — KEV 3 Aug; Hotfix 2 released 6 Aug

items.title: August ICS Patch Tuesday: Siemens, Schneider, Aveva and Phoenix Contact ship a new round of fixes
items.content_text: This week’s ICS Patch Tuesday saw Siemens, Schneider Electric, Aveva and Phoenix Contact publish fresh advisories across their product lines. Siemens led with roughly ten advisories, including a maximum-severity missing-authentication flaw that lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker run code on affected industrial-edge/IoT gear, a critical code-execution bug in its Siveillance video-management servers, and high-severity issues in Solid Edge, Simcenter, the Siemens License Server and Logo! Soft Comfort. Schneider, Aveva and Phoenix Contact addressed additional flaws in engineering and SCADA software. No public exploitation is reported yet, but the unauthenticated code-execution criticals warrant prompt triage on any exposed deployment — engineering workstations and edge devices bridging the plant floor first.

items.title: Rockwell FactoryTalk Services Platform auth-bypass lets a low-priv user impersonate anyone
items.content_text: CISA advisory ICSA-26-202-07 (21 July) describes a JWT signature-validation bypass in Rockwell Automation’s FactoryTalk Services Platform during Okta-based web authentication: because the token is accepted with “alg: none”, a low-privileged authenticated user can forge a token and impersonate any authorized user, including administrators. It is rated CVSS v3 7.8 / v4 8.8 and used primarily in critical manufacturing worldwide. FactoryTalk Services Platform underpins identity and access across the Rockwell OT stack, so a privilege-escalation-to-admin flaw there is a foothold into the software layer that governs engineering and operations. No public exploitation is reported; apply Rockwell’s fix.

items.title: New CISA advisory covers ABB Ability zenon SCADA/HMI — check your version exposure
items.content_text: CISA published ICSA-26-218-01 on 6 August covering vulnerabilities in ABB’s Ability zenon SCADA/HMI platform, widely used to visualize and supervise manufacturing lines and utilities. zenon sits at the operator layer that runs and monitors the process, so a weakness there can affect visibility and control of production. Affected versions, CVSS scoring and specific mitigations are detailed in the CISA advisory — consult it directly and map it to your deployed zenon runtime and engineering installations before acting. No public exploitation is reported at publication.

items.title: Fairlife’s 8-K puts SEC cyber-incident disclosure back on the plant manager’s radar
items.content_text: Coca-Cola’s prompt SEC filing over the Fairlife ransomware attack is a live example of how material cyber incidents at manufacturers now trigger securities-disclosure obligations, not just IR and recovery. For publicly-traded manufacturers and their suppliers, an OT-impacting incident that halts production can be material, so legal, finance and security need a pre-agreed process to assess materiality and disclose on a tight timeline — before the incident forces the question.
